title: Sugarcane Red Rot — Recognition and Prevention
topic: red rot, fungal disease, stalk rot
content:
Red rot, caused by the fungus Colletotrichum falcatum, is one of the most serious diseases of sugarcane. Externally, infected canes may show drying/withering of leaves starting from the top, and a distinctive alcohol-like smell when the stalk is split open. Internally, the characteristic sign is reddening of the stalk tissue with white patches crossing the red discoloration (visible when a cane is cut lengthwise).

The disease commonly spreads through infected seed cane (setts) used for planting, so using disease-free, certified seed material is one of the most effective preventive steps. The fungus can also survive in infected crop residue left in the field, so removing and destroying (not composting) severely infected canes and residue reduces carryover to the next crop.

Waterlogged conditions and stressed, weak canes are more susceptible, so proper drainage and balanced nutrition (avoiding both nutrient deficiency and excess nitrogen, which promotes soft, susceptible growth) support natural resistance.

Once a field shows significant red rot, there is no effective in-season cure — management is primarily preventive (clean seed, field sanitation, resistant varieties where available, and crop rotation with a non-host crop for at least one season before replanting sugarcane in a badly affected field).
